⛽️ Ten-Day Ceasefire, Nine Days of Bombing

For the ninth straight day, the US is bombing Iran while “exploring diplomatic options” through Qatar and Pakistan, who are pushing a 10‑day ceasefire to restore the pre–July 9 status quo in the Strait of Hormuz. 

Washington wants Iran to stop hitting shipping and reopen the chokepoint; Tehran insists it has every right to “manage” traffic and keeps firing on US bases in Kuwait, Jordan, Bahrain and Iraq. On the ground that means a blown‑up bridge near Bandar Abbas, damaged radio stations in Hormozgan, and a growing tally of dead and wounded on both sides.

The war is spilling out of Hormuz. Iran‑backed Houthis now threaten a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, putting Red Sea oil flows at risk and sending Brent crude twitching between fear and denial. 

US gasoline prices have jumped back above $4 a gallon, which is basically a negative campaign ad for Trump running on “America First” while Americans pay more for every commute. 

One fifth of the world’s oil and gas used to move through Hormuz; now traffic is down to levels last seen at the peak of the spring escalation, with some tankers turning off transponders like teenagers sneaking out at night.

The tit‑for‑tat is getting bloodier. Seventeen US service members are now dead in this war, including two killed in Jordan and one in Iraq in the last 48 hours, as Iran keeps hitting US positions and the Pentagon answers with more strikes on missile sites and comms networks. 

Trump says the latest bombardments were “in honor” of the troops killed and repeats the magic line that they died “so that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” as if bombing refineries and bridges directly translates into nonproliferation. 

Tehran says over 50 Iranians are dead and more than 500 wounded since this flare‑up began less than two weeks ago — but those numbers are background noise in US politics until the body bags carry American flags.

In Tehran, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi tries to have it both ways: Iran “won’t abandon diplomacy,” but also won’t return to talks “under bombardment.” 

He openly boasts that Iran’s actions in Hormuz “made us a global player,” spelling out what everyone already knows: the strait is leverage, not just geography. 

Marco Rubio, now secretary of state, claims Iran is “sending signals it wants to negotiate” and that the regime is split between deal‑makers and hardliners — the same comforting fairy tale US officials always tell themselves before the next round of escalation.

On TV, Washington insists it wants to “stop the war.” In reality, the US is flying in more F‑35s, F‑16s and refueling tankers and thickening its footprint across the Gulf. 

Iran’s parliament speaker shrugs that they’ve “become experts” at reading these moves and have “prepared accordingly” — code for more missiles, more drones, more ways to bleed American forces without triggering a full invasion. 

Kuwait, supposedly a protected partner, is now absorbing some of the worst Iranian attacks, with major energy sites evacuated and power and desalination plants hit.

Israel, as usual, is the loudest bystander. Netanyahu’s ministers are already threatening that if Iran “makes the mistake” of attacking Israel directly, they’ll respond with more force than in the last campaign — as if the region can absorb yet another “more force” round on top of Gaza, Lebanon and now Hormuz. 

Meanwhile, mediators float a 10‑day pause like a trial coupon for de‑escalation, while both sides use the breathing room to reload.

Iran uses Hormuz and proxies to prove it can raise the price of ignoring it. The US uses airstrikes to prove it’s still the sheriff.

Oil markets wobble, gas spikes, and ordinary people in Iran, the Gulf and the US eat the cost.

If this is what “deterrence” looks like, the only thing being deterred is any illusion that someone in charge actually wants this war to end — not just be managed.

🔔 Bitcoin price nears Fidelity’s power law support: Accumulation zone or missing catalyst? 

📌 On his power law model, a logarithmic chart that bounds Bitcoin’s entire price history between an upper resistance curve, a middle trendline, and a lower support curve, the floor currently sits near 58,000 dollars. That lower line has caught every major Bitcoin bottom since 2015. Timmer’s label for the zone the market has now entered is unambiguous: accumulation. His caveat is just as unambiguous: he sees no catalyst for a reversal, and he is not calling a bottom.

⚠️ That combination, a historically reliable floor approaching and a strategist refusing to ring the bell, is the most honest summary of the Bitcoin market in July 2026. The asset is coming off its worst quarter since the 2022 bear market, spot ETFs just recorded their largest quarterly outflow since launch, the speculative premium that carried the price past 120,000 dollars last year has evaporated, and the fast money has visibly rotated elsewhere, first into gold, then into semiconductor stocks. And yet the two quantitative measures Timmer trusts most, the deviation from the power law trendline and the Bitcoin-to-gold ratio, have both sunk to depths recorded at exactly two prior moments: the 2018 low and the 2022 low. Both of those moments were generational buying opportunities. Both also felt like the end of the world at the time.

🔖 This feature takes the model seriously in both directions: what the power law actually says, why its track record earns attention, and why the missing-catalyst objection is not a hedge but the core of the analysis.

➡️ When does a stablecoin become cash?

A stablecoin can trade at one dollar without being treated as cash inside the financial system.

That distinction is becoming one of the next major regulatory questions.

In written input to the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Ripple asked for qualified payment stablecoins to be recognised consistently as allowable assets, cash equivalents and eligible reserve assets in broker-dealer rules.

The request sounds technical. Its effects are not.

Classification determines:

- whether a financial firm can hold the asset as collateral
- how much capital must sit against it
- how customer assets are protected
- whether the token can move efficiently through regulated infrastructure

Stablecoin adoption will not be decided by transaction speed alone.

It will also be decided by the balance-sheet category regulators place around it.

The token can move in seconds. The legal classification decides where it is allowed to go.
